messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Fatima Nassir is a 21-year-old single woman of Lebanese descent who works as a database administrator at a mid-sized logistics firm in suburban Virginia. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 79, seeking help for the first time approximately fourteen months after returning from a deployment in which she served as a military intelligence analyst attached to a forward operating base in a conflict zone. What brought her through the clinic door, she explained quietly during intake, was a performance review at work in which her supervisor noted that she had stopped attending the after-hours system maintenance windows — late-night shifts that had once been a routine part of her role — and that her output, while technically precise, had become unusually narrow in scope. She had not told her supervisor why. She had not told anyone why.

The event that reorganised Fatima's inner world occurred during a night raid gone wrong. Her unit had been moving through a compound after dark when an explosion detonated roughly thirty metres ahead of her position. The concussive force knocked her to the ground. She remembers the weight of her kit pressing into her chest as she lay on the rubble, the smell of burning, the way her body refused to move for what felt like an enormous stretch of time, though she was later told it was seconds. Several of her colleagues sustained serious injuries. Fatima was physically unharmed, but the experience of lying pinned under that pressure in the dark, certain she was about to die, left an imprint that has not faded.

In the months that followed her discharge, the darkness itself became something she could not be neutral about. Going outside after sunset produces in her a state of vigilance so acute that she has effectively stopped doing it. She orders groceries online, declines social invitations that extend past early evening, and has rearranged her schedule so that her commute falls entirely within daylight hours. What frightened her most, she said, was not being able to see what was coming — and night, in her mind, had become inseparable from that compound and everything that happened inside it.

Physical exertion has taken on a similarly charged quality. Fatima had been a committed runner before her deployment. She has not run since returning. She described how elevated heart rate, the pressure in her chest during cardiovascular effort, and the breathlessness of pushing her body hard all produce a sensation she cannot tolerate — one that returns her, without warning, to the moment she was on the ground and could not get up. She has avoided the gym, declined a friend's invitation to a hiking trip, and quietly removed herself from any situation in which her body might be placed under sustained physical demand. She had come to believe that keeping herself physically calm was a form of safety, a way of ensuring that her body would not betray her by feeling the way it felt that night.

At home, Fatima has developed a pattern of cleaning and organising that she recognises, with some embarrassment, as excessive. Her apartment is immaculate. She reorganises her kitchen cabinets several times a week and has a precise system for her desk at work — cables routed identically each morning, folders arranged in a sequence she checks before she can begin her tasks. She described it not as a ritual but as a precondition: the sense that if her environment was ordered, something unpredictable was less likely to happen. Her colleagues have noticed. One made a joke about it. Fatima laughed along, then spent the rest of the afternoon unable to concentrate.

The occupational consequence has been the most concrete. Her refusal to attend night maintenance windows has meant that a junior colleague now covers shifts she was expected to manage, and she is aware that her standing on the team has quietly shifted. She worries her supervisor is losing confidence in her, but she has not been able to find the words to explain what happens to her when she imagines stepping outside into darkness and walking across a car park alone at eleven o'clock at night.

What Fatima is most afraid of, she said at the end of the intake session, is that there is no version of herself that gets to go back to who she was before. What she is hoping for, more tentatively, is that someone might tell her she is wrong about that.
